newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour may seek funds in snap budget - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour may seek funds in snap budget - analysts.

text.p: Britain's Labour party may go beyond its planned "windfall tax" on privatised utilities and introduce extra measures to raise revenue in a snap budget if it wins the forthcoming election, economists said on Tuesday.

"We reckon Labour will use an early budget to introduce a fiscal tightening of some four billion pounds, which would be applied to the 1997-98 fiscal year," said Jonathan Loynes, economist at HSBC Markets.

Economists said Britain's high level of public debt after four strong years of economic growth, coupled with the need to re-balance demand in the economy away from the consumer, could make a fiscal tightening tempting for a new Labour government.

Labour has pledged not to raise the main rates of income tax (which have not risen since 1977) but will turn to backdoor ways of raising revenues in the same way the Conservatives have done in recent decades.

If it wins the election expected on May 1, Labour has said it will hold a mini-budget within six weeks which will flesh out a windfall tax on profits of privatised utilities and use the money to help cut high levels of youth unemployment.

But, analysts say, the budget could embrace much more. The objective would not be to fill an alleged black hole in Labour's tax and spending plans, but to trim a burgeoning public debt bill and re-balance fiscal versus monetary policy.

Labour has pledged itself to the "golden rule" that current spending will be covered by available revenues, so the ratio of government debt to GDP will be stable on average over the economic cycle at a prudent and sensible level.
"Fiscal policy should be tightened so that the inflation objectives can be achieved without having to rely excessively on monetary policy," said Geoffrey Dicks, economist at NatWest Markets.

Without fiscal tightening analysts said there is a danger the pound's relentless rise on world markets quickens, encouraged by a more Europe-friendly government and the rises in interest rates needed if monetary policy takes all the strain of keeping inflation under the 2.5 percent target.

"A fiscal tightening so quickly after an election may be politically unpopular but if tightening is needed it is best to do it five years before the next election and blame it on the previous government's mismanagement," said Loynes of HSBC.

"The alternative to tax measures is probably mortgage rate rises -- which are highly unpopular," Loynes added. British base lending rates are currently at 6.0 percent, but markets are pricing in a rise to around 6.75 percent by the end of 1997.
Economists said Labour will not just inherit the problem of a strong pound if it wins the election, but also public finances which need more revenue and less spending.

With the public sector borrowing requirement at just over five percent of GDP last year, analysts warned that high public debt appears to have an in-built structural component, which is not set to disappear at the peak of the output cycle.

So while Britain may qualify for European economic and monetary union after half a decade of above-trend economic growth, fiscal tightening is needed to ensure debt does not climb sharply when the economy next enters a downturn.

Economists top recommendation for a new Labour government looking to raise revenue to balance the books would be to further restrict, or abolish, mortgage interest relief at source (MIRAS), a much criticised tax subsidy for home buyers.

Abolishing MIRAS would raise an extra 2.4 billion sterling of revenue but would also mimic a monetary tightening, being roughly equivalent to a 0.75 percent rise in mortgage rates, Dicks of NatWest said.

"This would take the steam out of the housing market and, by signalling that base rates would not need to rise above 6.0 percent, provide a correction to sterling's strength. It is not often that one single policy measure fulfils so many objectives. Labour should go for it," Dicks argues.
